Lessons.Title: Combining Polynomials
ExplanationParagraphs: Source-aligned goals: Comprehend that when polynomials are combined by addition, subtraction, or multiplication, the result is a polynomial. Justify (orally) conclusions about what happens when integers or polynomials are combined using arithmetic operations.

Sums, differences and products of polynomials remain polynomials. Combine like powers only when adding or subtracting; use distribution when multiplying. Degree of a product generally adds nonzero factor degrees, while addition may cancel leading terms and lower the result degree.

Source activity 4.1: Notice and Wonder: What Can Happen to Integers: What do you notice? What do you wonder? \(7 \boldcdot 9 = 63\) \(7 - 9 = \text-2\) \(\frac{7}{9} = 0.777 \ldots\) Explain the mathematical model, verify the relevant result and have a teacher inspect original diagrams or discussion evidence.

Source activity 4.2: Experimenting with Integers: Which of these statements are true? Give reasons in support of your answer. If you add two even numbers, you’ll always get an even number. If you subtract an even number from another even number, you’ll always get an even number. If you add two odd numbers, you’ll always get an odd number. If you subtract an odd number from another odd number, you’ll always get an odd number.… Explain the mathematical model, verify the relevant result and have a teacher inspect original diagrams or discussion evidence.

Source activity 4.3: Experimenting with Polynomials: Here are some questions about polynomials. You and a partner will work on one of these questions. If you add or subtract two polynomials, will you always get a polynomial? If you multiply two polynomials, will you always get a polynomial? Try combining some polynomials to answer your question. Use the ones given by your teacher or make up your own polynomials. Keep a record of… Explain the mathematical model, verify the relevant result and have a teacher inspect original diagrams or discussion evidence.

Practice Problem 1: Here are two expressions whose product is a new expression, \(A\). \(\displaystyle (5x^4 + \boxed{\phantom{33}}x^3)(4x^{\boxed{\phantom{3}}} - 6) = A\) Andre says that any real number can go in either of the boxes and \(A\) will be a polynomial. Is he correct? Explain your reasoning. Preserve original numbers, constraints and representations in a student practice task.

Practice Problem 2: Lin divides the polynomial \(2x^2 - 4x + 1\) by 4 and gets \(0.5x^2 - x + 0.25\). Is \(0.5x^2 - x + 0.25\) a polynomial? Explain your thinking. Preserve original numbers, constraints and representations in a student practice task.
Practice Problem 3: What is the result when any 2 integers are multiplied? Preserve original numbers, constraints and representations in a student practice task.

Practice Problem 4: Clare wants to make an open-top box by cutting out corners of a 30 inch by 25 inch piece of poster board and then folding up the sides. The volume \(V(x)\) in cubic inches of the open-top box is a function of the side length \(x\) in inches of the square cutouts. Write an expression for \(V(x)\). What is a reasonable… Preserve original numbers, constraints and representations in a student practice task.

Practice Problem 5: Identify the degree, leading coefficient, and constant value of each of the following polynomials. \(f(x)=2x^5 - 8 x^2 - x - 6\) \(h(x)=x^3 - 7 x^2 - x + 2\) \(g(x)=5 x^2-4 x^3 + 2x +5.4\) Preserve original numbers, constraints and representations in a student practice task.
Practice Problem 6: Which point is a relative minimum? Preserve original numbers, constraints and representations in a student practice task.
Edulytics independent cool-down: Subtract (2x^2+3x-1) from (5x^2-x+4). Expected reasoning or answer: 3x^2-4x+5.
